On a conjecture of Andrews and Bachraoui

Koustav Banerjee , Kathrin Bringmann and William Keith Address: University of Cologne, Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Weyertal 86-90, 50931 Cologne, Germany Email address: kbanerj1@uni-koeln.de Email address: kbringma@uni-koeln.de Address: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Michigan Tech, Houghton, MI 49931-1295 Email address: wjkeith@mtu.edu
Abstract.

Recently, Andrews and Bachraoui considered a generating function Fk,m​(q)F_{k,m}(q) associated with certain two-color partitions, and conjectured that this function has non-negative coefficients for m=1m=1. They showed this property for 1≤k≤41\leq k\leq 4. In this note, we prove that Fk,1​(q)F_{k,1}(q) has non-negative coefficients for 5≤k≤105\leq k\leq 10. Moreover, we show that, as k→∞k\to\infty, Fk,1​(q)F_{k,1}(q) is related to Ramanujan’s third order mock theta function ω⁡(q){\omega}(q) and to quotients of certain qq-binomial coefficients.

Key words and phrases: 
mock theta functions, partitions, qq-series.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05A17, 11P81.

1. Introduction and Statement of Results

Throughout let (a)n=(a,q)n:=∏j=0n−1(1−a​qj)(a)_{n}=(a;q)_{n}:=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1-aq^{j}) for n∈ℕ0∪{∞}n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\cup\{\infty\}. Moreover let (a1,…,aℓ)n=(a1,…,aℓ;q)n:=(a1)n⋯(aℓ)n(a_{1},...,a_{\ell})_{n}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{\ell};q)_{n}:=(a_{1})_{n}\cdots(a_{\ell})_{n} for ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}. Andrews and Bachraoui [3, Conjecture 2.8 and Conjecture 2.9] conjectured that for k,m∈ℕk,m\in\mathbb{N} and for k=2,m=4k=2,m=4, the coefficients of the qq-series

∑n≥0(q2​n+2,q2​n+2​k,q2)∞(q2​n+1,q2)∞2​qm⁡(2​n+1)=:∑n≥0ck,m​(n)​qn=:Fk,m​(q)\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{\left(q^{2n+2},q^{2n+2k};q^{2}\right)_{\infty}}{\left(q^{2n+1};q^{2}\right)^{2}_{\infty}}q^{m(2n+1)}=:\sum_{n\geq 0}c_{k,m}(n)q^{n}=:F_{k,m}(q)

are positive. Note that for m=1m=1, we have

(1.1) Fk,1​(q)=∑n≥0(q2​n+2,q2​n+2​k,q2)∞(q2​n+1,q2)∞2​q2​n+1.F_{k,1}(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{\left(q^{2n+2},q^{2n+2k};q^{2}\right)_{\infty}}{\left(q^{2n+1};q^{2}\right)^{2}_{\infty}}q^{2n+1}.

Andrews and Bachraoui [3, (2.2), (2.3), (2.5), Theorem 2.6] proved that ck,1​(n)>0c_{k,1}(n)>0 for n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} and 1≤k≤41\leq k\leq 4. Moreover they proposed the following conjecture (see [3, Conjecture 2.8]), which we partially prove in this paper.

Conjecture 1.1.

For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, ck,1​(n)>0c_{k,1}(n)>0.

To state our theorems, for A⁡(q)=∑n≥0a⁡(n)​qnA(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}a(n)q^{n} we mean, by A⁡(q)⪰0A(q)\succeq 0 (resp. A⁡(q)≻0A(q)\succ 0) that a⁡(n)≥0a(n)\geq 0 (resp. a⁡(n)>0a(n)>0) for n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}.

Theorem 1.2.

For k∈{5,6,7}k\in\{5,6,7\}, we have Fk,1​(q)⪰0F_{k,1}(q)\succeq 0.

Using a computational approach we extend this to k≤10k\leq 10.

Theorem 1.3.

For k∈{8,9,10}k\in\{8,9,10\}, we have Fk,1​(q)⪰0F_{k,1}(q)\succeq 0.

Our next result relates Fk,1F_{k,1} to the mock theta function ω\omega of Ramanujan [5]

(1.2) ω⁡(q):=∑n≥0q2​n​(n+1)(q,q2)n+12.\omega(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{2n(n+1)}}{\left(q;q^{2}\right)^{2}_{n+1}}.
Theorem 1.4.

We have

limk→∞Fk,1​(q)=q​ω​(q).\lim_{k\to\infty}F_{k,1}(q)=q\omega(q).

In the following theorem, we obtain more information about the function that prevents Fk,1​(q)F_{k,1}(q) from agreeing with q​ω​(q)q{\omega}(q). To state our result, for A⁡(q)=∑n≥0a⁡(n)​qnA(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}a(n)q^{n} and m∈ℕ0m\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, define

coeff[qm]⁡A⁡(q):=a⁡(m).\operatorname{coeff}_{\left[q^{m}\right]}A(q):=a(m).
Theorem 1.5.

For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, we have

q​ω​(q)−Fk,1​(q)=q2​k+1​Ek​(q)​with​Ek​(q)∈ℤ⁡[[q]]​and​coeff[q0]​Ek​(q)=1.q\omega(q)-F_{k,1}(q)=q^{2k+1}E_{k}(q)\ \text{with}\ E_{k}(q)\in\mathbb{Z}[[q]]\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{coeff}_{\left[q^{0}\right]}E_{k}(q)=1.

Theorem 1.5 immediately implies the following.

Corollary 1.6.

For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and 1≤m≤k1\leq m\leq k, we have

coeff[qm]⁡(q​ω​(q)−Fk,1​(q))=0for​ 1≤m≤2​k.\operatorname{coeff}_{\left[q^{m}\right]}\left(q\omega(q)-F_{k,1}(q)\right)=0\ \ \text{for}\ \ 1\leq m\leq 2k.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall some standard qq-series transformations and define notation. In Section 3 we transform Fk,1​(q)F_{k,1}(q) into certain forms which assist in proving Theorems 1.2, 1.4, and 1.5. In Section 4, we prove Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3, showing the positivity of the coefficients of Fk,1​(q)F_{k,1}(q) for 5≤k≤105\leq k\leq 10. Next, we prove Theorem 1.4, and Theorem 1.5, exhibiting the relations between Fk,1F_{k,1} and the third order mock theta function ω\omega. Finally, in Section 5, we presents a few plausible approaches to address Conjecture 1.1.

3. Some qq-series transformations

The following lemma is a key step for proving Theorem 1.2.

Lemma 3.1.

For k∈ℕ≥3k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}, we have

Proof.

Using (1.1), we obtain

Applying Lemma 2.1 with q↦q2q\mapsto q^{2}, a=b=qa=b=q, c=q2​kc=q^{2k}, and t=q2t=q^{2}, we have

∑n≥0(q,q2)n2​q2​n(q2,q2​k,q2)n=(q2​k−1,q3,q2)∞(q2​k,q2,q2)∞​∑n≥0(q4−2​k,q,q2)n(q2,q3,q2)n​q(2​k−1)​n.\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{\left(q;q^{2}\right)^{2}_{n}q^{2n}}{\left(q^{2},q^{2k};q^{2}\right)_{n}}=\frac{\left(q^{2k-1},q^{3};q^{2}\right)_{\infty}}{\left(q^{2k},q^{2};q^{2}\right)_{\infty}}\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{\left(q^{4-2k},q;q^{2}\right)_{n}}{\left(q^{2},q^{3};q^{2}\right)_{n}}q^{(2k-1)n}.

Fk,1​(q)=q(1−q)​(q,q2)k−1​(1+(1−q)​∑n=1k−2(q4−2​k,q2)n(q2,q2)n​q(2​k−1)​n1−q2​n+1).\displaystyle F_{k,1}(q)=\frac{q}{\left(1-q\right)\left(q;q^{2}\right)_{k-1}}\left(1+\left(1-q\right)\sum_{n=1}^{k-2}\frac{\left(q^{4-2k};q^{2}\right)_{n}}{\left(q^{2};q^{2}\right)_{n}}\frac{q^{(2k-1)n}}{1-q^{2n+1}}\right).

11−q​(1+q4+q6+q101−q9−1+q5+q91−q7)⪰0.\frac{1}{1-q}\left(\frac{1+q^{4}+q^{6}+q^{10}}{1-q^{9}}-\frac{1+q^{5}+q^{9}}{1-q^{7}}\right)\succeq 0.

We write

q101−q9=−q+q1−q9,q91−q7=−q2+q21−q7.\frac{q^{10}}{1-q^{9}}=-q+\frac{q}{1-q^{9}},\quad\frac{q^{9}}{1-q^{7}}=-q^{2}+\frac{q^{2}}{1-q^{7}}.

Thus we need to show that

11−q​(−q+q2+1+q+q4+q61−q9−1+q2+q51−q7)⪰0.\frac{1}{1-q}\left(-q+q^{2}+\frac{1+q+q^{4}+q^{6}}{1-q^{9}}-\frac{1+q^{2}+q^{5}}{1-q^{7}}\right)\succeq 0.

We combine

+q+q4+q6−q9−+q2+q5−q7\displaystyle\frac{1\!+\!q\!+\!q^{4}\!+\!q^{6}}{1\!-\!q^{9}}\!-\!\frac{1\!+\!q^{2}\!+\!q^{5}}{1\!-\!q^{7}} =(−q)​q​(+q3+q5−q7−q12)(−q7)​(−q9).\displaystyle=\frac{\left(1\!-\!q\right)q\left(1\!+\!q^{3}\!+\!q^{5}\!-\!q^{7}\!-\!q^{12}\right)}{\left(1\!-\!q^{7}\right)\left(1\!-\!q^{9}\right)}.

So we need

−1+1+q3+q5−q7−q12(1−q7)​(1−q9)⪰0.-1+\frac{1+q^{3}+q^{5}-q^{7}-q^{12}}{\left(1-q^{7}\right)\left(1-q^{9}\right)}\succeq 0.

It is not hard to see that the constant term of the left-hand side vanishes. Thus it is enough to show that

1+q3−q7−q12(1−q7)​(1−q9)=11−q9+q31−q7⪰0\frac{1+q^{3}-q^{7}-q^{12}}{\left(1-q^{7}\right)\left(1-q^{9}\right)}=\frac{1}{1-q^{9}}+\frac{q^{3}}{1-q^{7}}\succeq 0

which holds. thus concludes the proof for k=7k=7. ∎

Next, we prove Theorem 1.3.

Proof of Theorem 1.3. Throughout the proof, k∈{8,9,10}k\!\in\!\{8,9,10\}. We begin by establishing an alternative form for Fk,1​(q)F_{k,1}(q). To make the powers in the inner sum of Lemma 3.1 more explicitly positive, we distribute powers of qq. For this, we write

(q4−2​k,q2)n​q(2​k−1)​n=(−1)n​(q2​k−2​n−2,q2)n​qn2+2​n.\displaystyle\left(q^{4-2k};q^{2}\right)_{n}q^{(2k-1)n}=(-1)^{n}\left(q^{2k-2n-2};q^{2}\right)_{n}q^{n^{2}+2n}.

Plugging this into Lemma 3.1, we obtain

=1(q,q2)k−1​∑n=0k−2(−1)n​(q2​k−2​n−2,q2)n​q(n+1)2(1−q2​n+1)​(q2,q2)n\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(q;q^{2})_{k-1}}\!\sum_{n=0}^{k-2}\!\frac{(-1)^{n}\left(q^{2k-2n-2};q^{2}\right)_{n}q^{(n+1)^{2}}}{(1-q^{2n+1})(q^{2};q^{2})_{n}}
=1(q,q2)k−1​∑n=0k−2[k−2n]q2​(−1)n​q(n+1)2−q2​n+1.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(q;q^{2})_{k-1}}\!\sum_{n=0}^{k-2}\!\begin{bmatrix}k-2\\ n\end{bmatrix}_{q^{2}}\!\!\!\frac{(-1)^{n}q^{(n+1)^{2}}}{1\!-\!q^{2n+1}}.

Plugging this into (4.12), we conclude the proof. ∎

5. Potential extensions of current approaches

Each of the approaches employed in this paper runs into difficulties, which we now discuss, followed by some suggestions on extensions or alternatives.

In the proof of Theorem 1.2, for k=5k=5, we first simplify [k−2n]q2[\begin{smallmatrix}k-2\\ n\end{smallmatrix}]_{q^{2}}, then do long division and combine. However we are unable to find a uniform process of simplification, as shown in the proof of Theorem 1.2 for k∈{6,7}k\in\{6,7\}. If a persistent pattern could be found then the entire conjecture might be provable in this way.

In the proof of Theorem 1.3, the calculation is algorithmic but the lcm grows exponentially in kk. For k=11k=11 we are unable to continue. A more careful choice of where to cancel might allow further calculation; sufficient systematic insight, possibly including some combinatorial injections, might even be able to fully establish the conjecture. We make the following connection with qq-binomial quotients, which may hold independent interest for some readers. Recall Lemma 3.2

(5.1) Fk,1​(q)=∑n≥0(q2​k−1,q2)n​qn+1(q,q2)n+1=:∑n≥0Gk,n​(q)​qn+1.F_{k,1}(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{\left(q^{2k-1};q^{2}\right)_{n}q^{n+1}}{\left(q;q^{2}\right)_{n+1}}=:\sum_{n\geq 0}G_{k,n}(q)q^{n+1}.

We make the following refined conjecture, which would in turn imply Conjecture 1.1. Next, we rewrite Gk,n​(q)G_{k,n}(q) as a quotient of qq-binomials.

(5.2) Gk,n​(q)=11−q2​n+1​[2​k+2​n−22​n]q[k+n−1n]q2.G_{k,n}(q)=\frac{1}{1-q^{2n+1}}\frac{\begin{bmatrix}2k+2n-2\\ 2n\end{bmatrix}_{q}}{\begin{bmatrix}k+n-1\\ n\end{bmatrix}_{q^{2}}}.
Conjecture 5.1.

We have Gk,n​(q)⪰0G_{k,n}(q)\succeq 0.

The form given in (5.2), the symmetry of qq-binomial coefficients about their central peaks, and computational data suggest the following further conjecture:

Conjecture 5.2.

For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, k≥n+1k\geq n+1, we have

Gk,n−Gk+1,n−1⪰0.G_{k,n}-G_{k+1,n-1}\succeq 0.

We can establish the following.

Lemma 5.3.

For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, Gn+2−j,n=Gn+2,n−jG_{n+2-j,n}=G_{n+2,n-j}.

Proof.

Using (5.1) with k=n−j+2k=n-j+2 and then using (5.1) with k=n+2k=n+2 and n↦n−jn\mapsto n-j, we conclude the proof. ∎

Since Gk,0​(q)=11−qG_{k,0}(q)=\frac{1}{1-q} has nonnegative coefficients for all kk, it follows from Lemma 5.3 that Conjecture 5.2 would imply the nonnegativity of all Gk,nG_{k,n} and hence Conjecture 1.1. Lemma 5.3 also has the consequence that if we can show that Gk,n⪰0G_{k,n}\succeq 0 for each kk and 0≤n≤k−20\leq n\leq k-2, then all Gk,n⪰0G_{k,n}\succeq 0 and Conjecture 1.1 would be proved. Finally, the forms exhibited in the proof of Theorem 1.2, along with computational evidence, further suggest the following conjecture, which would also be sufficient to establish the positivity of Fk,1​(q)F_{k,1}(q):

Conjecture 5.4.

We have Gk,n​(q)=∑j=0nzk,j​(q)1−q2​j+1G_{k,n}(q)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{z_{k,j}(q)}{1-q^{2j+1}} where all zk,j​(q)z_{k,j}(q) have nonnegative coefficients.
